Learning Objectives
Describe the high-, mid-, and low-specificity fractures associated with child abuse.
Describe the differential diagnosis for child abuse.
Describe the indications for and content of a child abuse workup.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Fractures are a frequent physical finding in patients with child abuse, second in incidence to cutaneous
soft-tissue injuries.
Until children can walk on their own, they are unlikely to engage in activities in which an accidental injury
can occur.

Fractures are a frequent physical examination finding in patients with child abuse, second in
incidence to cutaneous soft-tissue injuries.1 As many as 55% of physically abused children have
sustained an inflicted fracture.2,3 These children generally are quite young: 85% of nonaccidental
fractures are diagnosed in children younger than 3 years, with 69% diagnosed in children younger
than 12 months.2,4,5 Developmental stage consistent with independent ambulation is an important
factor: Until children can walk on their own, they are far less likely to engage in activities in which an
accidental injury can occur.
Epidemiology
No fracture pattern, location, or morphology is pathognomonic for child abuse.
Certain fractures and fracture patterns may be suggestive of nonaccidental trauma (Resource 1).

Epidemiology
Despite being a common manifestation of nonaccidental trauma, fractures may pose a diagnostic
dilemma. No fracture pattern, location, or morphology is pathognomonic for child abuse. However,
certain fractures and fracture patterns may be suggestive of nonaccidental trauma.2-20 Recognition
of these fracture patterns is essential for early identification of nonaccidental trauma.
Understanding the differences between high-, mid-, and low-specificity fractures may aid in the
workup.
High-Specificity Fractures
21-23
Long bone fractures in nonambulatory children
Classic metaphyseal lesions (CMLs; corner fractures, bucket-handle fractures)
Rib fractures
Sternal, scapular, and pelvic fractures
Multiple fractures, especially in various stages of healing
Fractures associated with other injuries
Transphyseal distal humerus fractures
Long Bone Fractures in Nonambulatory Children
SEND FEEDBACK


Long Bone Fractures in Nonambulatory Children
Any long bone fracture (diaphyseal, metaphyseal, or physeal) in a child who is too young to walk
should raise concern for child abuse. A single, isolated, transverse long bone fracture is the most
common fracture pattern in patients with nonaccidental trauma, occurring in 13% of patients.2
Classic Metaphyseal Lesions

Classic Metaphyseal Lesions
(Figure 1)
CMLs, although relatively uncommon, are highly specific for child abuse, particularly if they are
observed in more than one long bone.3,24 CMLs account for as many as 28% of nonaccidental long
bone fractures.2,20,25 They are speculated to occur via combined traction and torsion, causing
shearing forces through the periphery of the metaphysis.26 However, an experimental porcine
model produced CMLs by applying a tensile stress through varus and valgus loading.27 Fragment
appearance on radiographs, the historical description of a CML, depends on the radiographic view.
On a tangential AP or lateral radiograph, the fracture appears wedge shaped at the edge of the
metaphysis (ie, corner fracture; Figure 2). On an oblique or angulated radiograph, curvilinear
fragments adjacent to the metaphysis are visible (ie, bucket-handle fracture; Figure 3). CMLs also
have a characteristic histologic appearance of subphyseal microfractures through the primary
spongiosa and calcified cartilage of the metaphysis28 .
Figure 1 Diagrammatic representation shows the relationship of the subperiosteal bone collar to a
metaphyseal lesion. A, A tangential view of the metaphyseal margin shows a fracture line (arrows)
that extends adjacent to the chondro-osseous junction centrally. Peripherally, the fracture line

Rib Fractures

Rib Fractures
Rib fractures also are highly specific for nonaccidental trauma. A classic pattern of three or four
posterior fractures of consecutive ribs, corresponding with the placement of the perpetrator’s
fingers while squeezing or shaking a child, has been described. However, a recent meta-analysis
showed anterior rib fractures to be most common in abuse, whereas the predictive value of
posterior rib fractures was inconsistent. Overall, the specific location of the rib fractures was not
directly correlated with the likelihood of abuse.12

Sternal, Scapular, and Pelvic Fractures

Sternal, Scapular, and Pelvic Fractures
Fractures of the sternum, scapula, and pelvis are rare in children and are almost always the result
of high-energy trauma. They should increase concern for abuse in the absence of a verifiable,
plausible mechanism of injury, such as a motor vehicle accident or a fall from a height.3,4,13,16,29,30
Multiple Fractures

Multiple Fractures
(Figure 4)
Multiple fractures, either acute or in various stages of healing, are highly specific for child
abuse.12,14,31 Fifty percent of abused children overall and 80% of those younger than 1 year are
diagnosed with more than one fracture.3,32,33 The odds ratio for child abuse is 4 to 6 for children
with three or more fractures compared with children with only one fracture6.

Fractures Associated with Other Injuries

Fractures Associated with Other Injuries
Acute or healing fractures diagnosed in combination with other corroborative injuries are indicative
of child abuse. Examples of other suspicious or sentinel injuries are burns, bruises, frenulum tears,
intracranial hemorrhage, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and abdominal or genital injury.34
Transphyseal Distal Humerus Fracture

Transphyseal Distal Humerus Fracture

This fracture pattern usually involves a displaced Salter-Harris type I fracture of the distal humeral
physis. It typically occurs in children younger than 1 year with a completely non-ossified distal
humeral epiphysis. Therefore, the entire distal fracture fragment is not observed on plain
radiographs, making diagnosis a challenge. These fractures often are missed completely or are
misdiagnosed as an elbow dislocation by novice clinicians (Figure 5). Subsequently, these fractures
often are diagnosed late after periosteal reaction is visible on plain radiographs (Figure 6).
Figure 5 Oblique (A) and AP (B) plain radiographs of an elbow demonstrate that the forearm is not
aligned with the humerus, which is characteristic of a transphyseal distal humerus fracture.
(Courtesy of Joshua Abzug, MD, Baltimore, MD.)

Mid-Specificity Fractures
Spinal fractures
Fractures of the hands and feet
Skull fractures
Clavicle fractures
Spinal Fractures

Spinal Fractures
Similar to fractures of the sternum and scapula, traumatic fractures of the spine are unusual in
children and typically are the result of a high-energy injury.
Fractures of the Hands and Feet

Fractures of the Hands and Feet
Accidental fractures of the hands and feet are uncommon in nonambulatory children and should
raise concern if observed in children younger than walking age.
Skull Fractures

Skull Fractures
Corroborative history is important in the evaluation of skull fractures because the most common
fracture pattern is the same in accidental and nonaccidental trauma: a simple, linear parietal
fracture.5,35,36

Clavicle Fractures

Clavicle Fractures
Fractures of the clavicle are a common result of birth trauma. In such patients, callus formation will
be visible on radiographs when the baby is 7 to 10 days old. In an infant older than 10 days, an
acute clavicle fracture without evidence of healing callus should raise concern for child abuse.
Isolated Long Bone Fracture in an Ambulatory Child Without a Plausible History

Isolated Long Bone Fracture in an Ambulatory Child Without a Plausible
History
This scenario presents a diagnostic challenge. A long bone fracture in an ambulatory child resulting
from an unwitnessed injury or for which no plausible explanation is given should raise concern for
child abuse. However, this situation is not as suspicious as a fracture in a nonambulatory child. In
the absence of corroborative skeletal survey findings or evidence of other injuries, a definitive
determination may be impossible.
Low-Specificity Fractures
Toddler fracture
Distal radial and ulnar torus fractures
Supracondylar humerus fractures
Toddler Fracture

Toddler Fracture
A patient with a toddler fracture typically presents with an isolated, nondisplaced spiral fracture of
the distal tibial metaphysis; however, such injuries also may be diaphyseal. Often, an oblique
radiograph of the tibia is required for adequate visualization. These fractures may result from
seemingly trivial injury. Parents often report a misstep off a stair or curb or a simple fall from
standing height. A well-documented etiology for this fracture pattern is a child getting his or her

foot caught along the edge of a playground slide while going down the slide seated on an adult’s
lap.37 Another low-specificity variation is a transverse or torus fracture of the proximal tibial
metaphysis caused by the recoil of a trampoline mat.38,39
Distal Radial and Ulnar Torus Fractures

Distal Radial and Ulnar Torus Fractures
Buckle fractures of the distal radius and ulna, which are the result of compressive forces, are
extremely common. They are almost always accidental, typically resulting from a fall onto an
outstretched arm or from running into a barrier with the arm outstretched.
Supracondylar Humerus Fractures

Supracondylar Humerus Fractures
Supracondylar humerus fractures typically are accidental and occur from a fall, often from
playground equipment or a trampoline.40-42
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Nonaccidental trauma should be suspected in any child with a high-specificity fracture pattern.21-23,43
Patient History

Patient History
A detailed history of the incident should be obtained from parents, caregivers, siblings, and
witnesses. If possible, each person should be interviewed separately. Typically, caregivers are
interviewed by multiple medical personnel. All inconsistencies and/or discrepancies in caregivers’
accounts should be noted. Circumstances that are red flags include inconsistencies, discrepancies,
or changes in caregivers’ accounts of the injury; unwitnessed injuries; injuries blamed on siblings;

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000035
11/21

injuries inconsistent with the stated mechanism of injury; a delay in seeking care; and a mechanism
of injury inconsistent with the child’s developmental stage.
Physical Examination
A thorough physical examination of the child by a non?orthopaedic surgeon is necessary to identify other
evidence of abuse, including skin bruising, abrasions, or scarring; retinal hemorrhages; intracranial
bleeds; or evidence of sexual abuse.
Skin lesions, including bruising and scarring, are the most common sign of nonaccidental trauma.
Fractures are the second most common.
Imaging Studies
21-23
Radiography

Radiography
A skeletal survey must be obtained in all children with a high-specificity fracture, evidence of
medical neglect, evidence of physical abuse, or a sentinel injury (Table 1). A skeletal survey should
be obtained for all children 1 year or younger with any long bone fracture, 18 months and younger
with a femoral fracture, and 2 years or younger with a humeral fracture. The skeletal survey should
consist of a skull series; an AP and lateral view of the thoracolumbar spine; and AP bilateral views of
the hands, feet, arms, forearms, thighs, and lower legs. These should be separate radiographs; a
babygram, in which one radiograph of the child’s entire skeleton is obtained on a long cassette, is
not detailed enough for a skeletal survey. A follow-up skeletal survey typically is performed 2 weeks
after presentation. New findings are observed in approximately one-quarter of patients on a follow-
up survey. Siblings of index patients who are younger than 2 years also should undergo a skeletal
survey.44

Magnetic Resonance Imaging

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is sensitive and specific for fractures in general but not sensitive for CMLs and rib fractures. In
addition, MRI is not routinely used to evaluate musculoskeletal injuries if nonaccidental trauma is
suspected. Although MRI does not involve radiation exposure, it often necessitates sedation or
general anesthesia in young children.
Bone Scintigraphy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Child Abuse (Nonaccidental Trauma)
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000035
13/21


Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy may be used as a screening test for children who are too young to localize pain.
Bone scintigraphy also is useful if clinical suspicion for fracture is high but plain radiographs are
negative. Bone scintigraphy is particularly useful in the diagnosis of posterior rib fractures and is
highly sensitive (but not specific) for areas of increased bone turnover; however, bone scans are
relatively expensive and involve radiation. In addition, fractures located near the physis are easy to
miss because the growth plate itself is extremely active metabolically and normally exhibits
increased uptake on a bone scan, which may mask increased uptake secondary to an adjacent
fracture. Therefore, bone scans are not routinely used to screen for musculoskeletal injuries if
nonaccidental trauma is suspected.
Ultrasonography

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is noninvasive, painless, and relatively inexpensive; does not involve radiation;
and does not require sedation. Ultrasonography is particularly useful in the diagnosis of
costochondral rib injuries and can depict subperiosteal hemorrhage, an early indicator of fracture,
before periosteal new bone is observed on plain radiographs.
Positron Emission Tomography

Positron Emission Tomography
Positron emission tomography is more sensitive than a skeletal survey for rib and spinal fractures
but is less sensitive for CMLs. Positron emission tomography involves radiation, and sedation or
general anesthesia typically is required. Therefore, positron emission tomography is not routinely
used in the diagnosis of nonaccidental trauma.
Other Studies


Other Studies
Bone mineral density scanning (ie, dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry [DEXA]) can differentiate injury
as a result of child abuse from osteogenesis imperfecta. Most children who are victims of abuse
have normal bone density that increases with age and growth, whereas children with osteogenesis
imperfecta are osteoporotic, with bone density that decreases as they age. Typically, a baseline
DEXA scan is obtained at presentation, with a follow-up scan obtained 4 to 6 months later for
comparison.
Differential Diagnosis
21,22,43,45
(Resource 2)
Various illnesses and disorders may be mistaken for child abuse and vice versa.
Usually, a careful patient history and physical examination in combination with judiciously ordered
laboratory and imaging studies can confirm the correct diagnosis.
The differential diagnosis for child abuse includes
Normal variants
Infants may exhibit transient metaphyseal cupping and spurring and periosteal new bone formation
along long bone cortices.
Birth trauma
This usually involves a fracture of the humerus or clavicle. Typically, a history of high birth weight
and/or difficult or traumatic delivery is noted. Callus should be visible on radiographs within 2 weeks
of age.
Caffey disease (infantile cortical hyperostosis)
This is a painful self-limited condition in children younger than 1 year. The appearance of Caffey
disease on radiographs is similar to that of periosteal new bone formation. Mandibular involvement is
characteristic.
Metabolic bone disease

Metabolic bone disease
Metabolic bone disease and inherited conditions of fragile bones may be mistaken for child abuse.
Rickets, osteogenesis imperfecta, renal disease, medications (such as corticosteroids or seizure
medications), or disuse osteopenia from not ambulating (eg, in cerebral palsy) may be included in
the differential diagnosis for fragile bones. In pathologic bone, fracture patterns may mimic those

highly specific for child abuse. A workup to rule out metabolic bone disease will potentially
decrease the incidence of erroneous reports, enable children to obtain necessary treatment, and
help address a possible metabolic bone disease if the issue arises in court. An initial metabolic bone
disease workup typically includes a simple set of laboratory tests, including 25-hydroxy vitamin D
level, blood urea nitrogen level, creatinine level, alkaline phosphatase level, calcium level, and
phosphorus level, and possibly a DEXA scan. 
Rickets
A family of conditions in which mineralization of the osteoid is abnormal
Diagnosis usually is made based on patient history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and
radiographs
On radiography, cupping and widening of the physes is characteristic of rickets.
Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease)
1. May be a difficult diagnosis to make
2. Osteogenesis imperfect has been mapped to two locations on two different genes (7 and 17) coding for
collagen type I.
3. Most cases are new mutations; often no family history of the disease is noted.
4. At least 19 types of osteogenesis imperfecta and many mutations of unknown importance have been
identified.
5. Wide variations exist in phenotype and gene expressivity.
6. Approximately one-half of patients have blue sclerae or dentinogenesis imperfecta.
7. DEXA scans are becoming a useful adjunct for diagnosing osteogenesis imperfecta. Bone mineral density
is almost always decreased in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta and continues to decline as they
age. Therefore, sequential DEXA scans, 4 to 6 months apart, are recommended.
8. Weeks to months may be required to diagnosis osteogenesis imperfecta, and parents of children with
undiagnosed osteogenesis imperfecta have been wrongfully suspected of child abuse; however, the
mandate as physicians is to err on the side of protecting the child.
9. Some child abuse experts maintain that children with osteogenesis imperfecta and other chronic
illnesses are more likely to be abused than other children; however, the literature is unclear.
10. An avulsion fracture of the olecranon apophysis is frequently observed in children with osteogenesis
imperfecta.
Leukemia
Osteolytic lesions, periosteal new bone, and diffuse osteopenia are observed on the radiographs of
children with leukemia. These children typically are systemically ill. Abnormalities on peripheral blood
smear and bone marrow biopsy are diagnostic.

Riley-Day syndrome (familial dysautonomia, congenital insensitivity to pain)
This autosomal recessive disorder is common in Ashkenazi Jews. Genetic testing for the syndrome is
available and sometimes reveals a positive family history. Patients typically have some cognitive,
developmental, and neurologic abnormalities and are prone to injury (including fracture) because of a
lack of protective pain response.
Menkes disease (copper deficiency)
This is an x-linked recessive disorder of copper metabolism. Patients have wormian bones of the skull
and characteristic laboratory values (decreased serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels).
Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency)
This disease is characterized by episodes of subperiosteal bleeding, subsequently leading to large
areas of subperiosteal calcification. Scurvy is rare in the United States and Europe.
Vitamin A intoxication
The disorder is characterized by a thickened periosteum, premature physeal closure, and widened
cranial sutures. The patient’s skin often has a yellow to orange tint. Increased serum vitamin A levels
are diagnostic.
Management
Reporting suspected child abuse is mandatory21-23 (Resource 3).
The orthopaedic surgeon is protected from litigation in reporting cases of suspected abuse.
Failure to report suspected abuse puts the affected child at a 30% to 50% risk of repeated abuse and a
5% to 10% risk of death.
In many states, after a report has been made, it cannot be retracted.
A multidisciplinary approach to reporting, including the input of a child abuse physician, is helpful.
The trend in many states is to maintain the family unit through investigation and intervention.
Many fractures resulting from child abuse have sufficiently healed at the time of presentation and do not
require management. Acute fractures typically can be managed via splinting or cast immobilization.
Early recognition and immediate hospital admission places the child in a safe, protected environment
that allows for additional evaluation of the child and the family.
Outcomes
Most fractures secondary to child abuse occur in very young children and show good healing and
remodeling potential.
